lesson.title: Creating the Remote Repository
lesson.summary: Understand creating the remote repository from first principles, with a small runnable example.

stage.name: Professional Practice
stage.subtitle: Book chapters 14–18
stage.description: Objects and patterns in the wider project: version control, testing, and automated builds.

payload.markdown: The --bare flag tells Git to initialize a repository without a working directory. Git will complain if you try to push to a repository that has not been created in this way.

payload.markdown: At the moment, only the root user can mess around under /var/git. I can change this by creating a user and a group named git and making it the directory’s owner:

$ sudo chown -R git:git /var/git

Providing Access to Users

payload.markdown: The owner of the bob user mentioned in the previous section can log in to the server and interact with the repository from his shell. Generally, though, you won’t want to provide shell access to all your users. In any case, most users will prefer to take advantage of Git’s distributed nature and to work locally with their cloned data.

payload.markdown: One way to grant a user SSH access is via public key authentication. To do this, you first need to acquire the user’s public SSH key. The user may already have this—on a Linux machine, he will probably find the key in the configuration directory, .ssh, in a file named id_rsa.pub. Otherwise, he can easily generate a new key. payload.markdown: As the repository administrator, I will have asked you for a copy of this key. Once I have it, I must add it to the git user’s SSH setup on the repository server. This is merely a matter of pasting the public key into the .ssh/authorized_keys file. I may need to create the .ssh configuration directory for the first key I set up (I am running these commands from the git user’s home directory):

blocks.text: As the repository administrator, I will have asked you for a copy of this key. Once I have it, I must add it to the git user’s SSH setup on the repository server. This is merely a matter of pasting the public key into the .ssh/authorized_keys file. I may need to create the .ssh configuration directory for the first key I set up (I am running these commands from the git user’s home directory):

payload.code:
$ mkdir .ssh
$ chmod 0700 .ssh
# create authorized_keys file and paste in the user's key:
$ vi .ssh/authorized_keys
$ chmod 0700 .ssh/authorized_keys

payload.text: Note A common cause of SSH access failure is the creation of configuration files with overly liberal permissions. The SSH configuration environment should be readable and writable to the account’s owner only. Pro OpenSSH by Michael Stahnke (Apress, 2005) covers SSH comprehensively.

🧠 Key concepts

items: Data Mapper: A layer that moves objects to and from storage without the object knowing SQL.
Git, CI & Build: Version control plus automated checks that run on every change.
Named Arguments: Passing arguments by parameter name, in any order, for readable calls.
Unit of Work: Tracking changes to many objects and writing them in a single transaction.
